fields.sample_size: interviews with households (the first author spoke in 2008 with women from 14 households, eight of them members of the Makina Women's Group), water company officials and former officials, water vendors and landlords, plus the second author's three years of living and working in Kibera; number of other interviews not stated
fields.effect_measure: qualitative case study with descriptive figures quoted from other sources (survey of 674 households in three Kenyan cities, UNDP 2006); no inferential statistics
fields.effect_estimate: Households in Kenyan slums spend about an hour on a good day (hours on a bad day) fetching 20-litre cans from vendors, an estimated 20% of income goes to water (UNDP 2006), Kibera (about 170,000 people on 250 ha; 60% of Nairobi lives in informal settlements) has infant and under-five mortality and bloody diarrhoea about three times the Nairobi average, and water costs some households nearly as much as rent; women curtail laundry, postpone baths and sometimes cut meals, and many store jerry cans in the home with likely contamination. Three phases of utility reform after the Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company was devolved from the City Council in 2002: Maji Bora Kibera (an association of water traders and landlords working with the company), a second experiment and a third phase with community involvement and elements of deliberative democracy; the arrangement with the vendors broke down in 2007 when police-led mass disconnections created mistrust. The authors conclude that institution-building proceeds by iterative experimentation and is buffeted by outside forces.

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a qualitative case study of access to water and utility reform in Kibera, Nairobi, based on interviews (14 households and officials, vendors, landlords) and long-term residence; read in full text 2026-10-04. Descriptive figures are quoted from other sources.
